title: NTA UGC NET English Full Mock Test #08
subtitle: 100 Questions · 200 Marks · Post-2018 NTA Pattern · Zero Answer Bias (25 A/B/C/D) · Reading Comprehension (Q91-100)

items.title: Mock #08 · Q1
items.stem:
Match List I with List II
List I (Author) – List II (Autobiography/Memoir)
(a) Pablo Neruda  (i) Under My Skin
(b) Graham Greene  (ii) Speak, Memory
(c) Doris Lessing  (iii) Memoirs
(d) Vladimir Nabokov  (iv) A Sort of Life
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Neruda wrote Memoirs, Greene A Sort of Life, Lessing Under My Skin, and Nabokov Speak, Memory.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q2
items.stem:
Robert Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy was published in 1621 and expanded and altered in
__________ subsequent editions
items.explanation: Following its first publication in 1621, Oxford scholar Robert Burton continually revised and expanded The Anatomy of Melancholy across five subsequent editions containing his authorial additions (1624, 1628, 1632, 1638, and the posthumous 1651 edition).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q3
items.stem:
Here are some characteristics of Morality Plays :
(1) They are dramatized allegories of the life of man.
(2) They depict man's temptation and sinning, his quest for salvation and his confrontation with Death.
(3) Though the hero represents Mankind, the other characters are by no means personifications, of virtues, vices and death.
(4) A character known as the Vice often plays the role of the hero, a predecessor of the Villain-hero in Elizabethan drama.

Find the correct combination according to the code :
items.explanation: Medieval morality plays such as Everyman and The Castle of Perseverance are dramatized allegories of human life (1) depicting temptation, sin, the quest for salvation, and the reckoning with Death (2), whereas the supporting figures are indeed personified virtues and vices.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q4
items.stem:
What this accoutred frowsty ____ is worth,

It pleases me to stand in silence here.
(Fill in the blank)
items.explanation: These lines occur in Stanza 6 of Philip Larkin's poem 'Church Going' (from The Less Deceived, 1955), where the skeptical modern speaker visits an empty country church and admits: 'For, though I've no idea / What this accoutred frowsty barn is worth, / It pleases me to stand in silence here.'

items.title: Mock #08 · Q5
items.stem:
Chronologically arrange the following works according to the year of publication.
A. Gauri Viswanathan’s Masks of Conquests.
B. Meenakshi Mukherjee’s The Twice Born Fiction.
C. G. N. Devy’s After Amnesia
D. M. K. Naik’s A History of Indian English Literature
E. Harish Trivedi’s Colonial Transactions
items.explanation: The publication years of these seminal critical studies in chronological order are: Meenakshi Mukherjee's The Twice Born Fiction (1971), M. K. Naik's A History of Indian English Literature (1982), Gauri Viswanathan's Masks of Conquest (1989), G. N. Devy's After Amnesia (1992), and Harish Trivedi's Colonial Transactions (1993). This yields the sequence B -> D -> A -> C -> E.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q6
items.meta: Unit X: Research Methods and Materials in English
items.stem: Hypothesis made during or after the research work is over, is known as:
items.explanation: A deductive hypothesis is formulated logically from broader theoretical propositions and tested during or concluding the empirical phase of investigation, verifying specific deductive conclusions against observed findings.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q7
items.stem:
Given below are two statements : One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.
Assertion (A): The Marxists represent Marxism as a scientific account of social change.
Reason (R): The Marxist ideology believes that culture is a mirror of social life and the artist is an engineer of the human soul educating the working classes.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
items.explanation: Orthodox Marxist theory presents historical materialism as a scientific account of social and economic change (Assertion A), and classical Marxist/Socialist Realist aesthetics views culture as a reflection ('mirror') of social reality and the writer as an 'engineer of the human soul' educating the proletariat (Reason R).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q8
items.stem:
Identify the novel with the wrong
subtitle listed below
options: Tess of the D'Urbervilles, A Pure Woman
The Mayor of Casterbridge, A Man of Character
Middlemarch, a Study of Provincial Life
items.explanation: George Eliot's 1866 industrial and political novel is titled Felix Holt, the Radical—not Felix Holt, the Socialist. The subtitles listed for Middlemarch, Tess of the d'Urbervilles, and The Mayor of Casterbridge are all accurate.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q9
items.stem:
Which of these may be said to be true of the journal published from Bowling Green University from 1969, which
carried essays on Spiderman comics, rock music, and detective films?
A. It sought to highlight the importance of popular culture.
B. It sought to highlight the importance of elite culture.
C. It sought to buttress the canon by making it more elitist.
D. It sought to break down the dominance of 'high' culture.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Journal of Popular Culture, published at Bowling Green State University, legitimized the academic study of everyday mass culture (A) and challenged the canonical monopoly of elite 'high' culture (D).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q10
items.stem:
Which of the following statements are correct about ‘Litotes’?
A. It contains an understatement for emphasis.
B. It is not opposite of hyperbole.
C. It is used with laconic intentions.
D. It is used with ironic intentions.
E. It is used in dramatic context.
items.explanation: Litotes is a figure of speech featuring intentional understatement achieved by negating the opposite (such as "he was not unhappy") (A), often chosen for its laconic restraint (C) and understated, ironic wit (D). Statement B is incorrect because litotes is precisely the rhetorical opposite of hyperbole (overstatement).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q11
items.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I (Concept/Idea):
A. Response to Stephen Gosson
B. The Individual Talent
C. Catharsis
D. Sweetness and Light

List II (Critic):
I. Aristotle
II. Matthew Arnold
III. T. S. Eliot
IV. Philip Sidney

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Sir Philip Sidney wrote An Apology for Poetry as a response to Stephen Gosson's The Schoole of Abuse (A-IV), T.S. Eliot wrote 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' (1919, B-III), Aristotle formulated the theory of tragedy and catharsis in Poetics (C-I), and Matthew Arnold popularized 'Sweetness and Light' in Culture and Anarchy (1869, D-II).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q12
items.stem:
"There is nothing outside the text"
is a key statement emanating from
items.explanation: 'There is nothing outside the text' ('Il n'y a pas de hors-texte') is Jacques Derrida's famous dictum from Of Grammatology (1967), a foundational statement of Deconstruction asserting that all meaning is mediated through linguistic signifiers and context.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q13
items.stem:
Which of the following have NOT been written by Mahesh Dattani?
A. Dance Like a Man
B. Fire and the Rain
C. On A Muggy Night in Mumbai
D. A Touch of Brightness
E. Bravely Fought the Queen
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Fire and the Rain (1998, B) was written by Girish Karnad and A Touch of Brightness (1968, D) was written by Partap Sharma. Dance Like a Man (1989), On a Muggy Night in Mumbai (1998), and Bravely Fought the Queen (1991) are plays by Mahesh Dattani.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q14
items.stem: While documenting, when is a block quotation used in prose?
options: If a quotation runs in more than two lines
If a quotation runs in more than five lines
If a quotation runs in more than three lines
If a quotation runs in more than four lines
items.explanation: According to the MLA Handbook (8th and 9th editions), a prose quotation that runs to more than four lines in the writer's text must be set off from the main text as an indented block quotation without quotation marks.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q15
items.stem:
Arrange the following critical texts chronologically on the basis of their publication:
A. The Historical Novel (George Lukacs)
B. The New Criticism (T.S. Eliot)
C. The Business of Criticism (Helen Gardner)
D. The Political Unconscious (Frederic Jameson)
E. Essays on Ideology (Louis Althusser)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The chronological order of critical texts is: T.S. Eliot's early essays associated with New Criticism (The Sacred Wood, 1920, B); Helen Gardner's The Business of Criticism (1959, C); György Lukács's The Historical Novel (English translation 1962, A); Fredric Jameson's The Political Unconscious (1981, D); and Louis Althusser's Essays on Ideology (1984, E).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q16
items.stem: A modem philosophical tendency which stresses the perceiver's role in determining meaning is known as
items.explanation: Founded by Edmund Husserl in the early twentieth century, phenomenology is the philosophical study of structures of consciousness as experienced from the first-person perspective, emphasizing the crucial role of the perceiver in interpreting and constituting meaning.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q17
items.stem:
Given below are two statements : One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.
Assertion (A): No piece of research will be the first of its kind
Reason (R): The reliability of progress in knowledge is dependent on the honesty of the researchers.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
items.explanation: All research builds on earlier work, and honesty of researchers matters for reliable knowledge, but honesty does not explain why no work is first.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q18
items.stem: Which of the following is the most accurate statement by W.E.B. Du Bois’s famous articulation of the ‘twoness’ of black Americans ?
options: “It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one’s self through the eyes of others.”
“This sense of always looking at one’s self, a peculiar sensation through the eyes of others, is double consciousness.”
“Through the eyes of others, this sense of always looking at one’s self, we acquire the double-consciousness.”
“This double consciousness, this sense of always looking at one’s self through the eyes of others, is a peculiar sensation.”
items.explanation: In The Souls of Black Folk Du Bois wrote: 'It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others.'

items.title: Mock #08 · Q19
items.stem:
Which of the following concepts are associated with the writings of Jean Baudrillard?
A. Hyperreality
B. Bricolage
C. Rhizome
D. Simulacra
E. Dispositif
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Hyperreality (A) and Simulacra (D) are the signature concepts of French postmodern theorist Jean Baudrillard, most famously elaborated in Simulacra and Simulation (1981). Bricolage is associated with Lévi-Strauss and Derrida, Rhizome with Deleuze and Guattari, and Dispositif with Foucault.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q20
items.stem:
Ideology and Ideological State
Apparatuses is an essay by
items.explanation: 'Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses' (1970) is a foundational structuralist-Marxist essay by French philosopher Louis Althusser, introducing the concept of ideological 'interpellation' and distinguishing between Repressive and Ideological State Apparatuses.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q21
items.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I
(A) Malcolm Bradbury
(B) David Lodge
(C) Kingsley Amis
(D) C P Snow

List II
(I) Masters
(II) Lucky Jim
(III) The History Man
(IV) Changing places

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: These classic British campus novels match as follows: Malcolm Bradbury's The History Man (1975, A-III), David Lodge's Changing Places (1975, B-IV), Kingsley Amis's Lucky Jim (1954, C-II), and C. P. Snow's The Masters (1951, D-I).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q22
items.stem: Poetry according to Sir Philip Sidney is of three kinds. They are
items.explanation: In An Apology for Poetry (The Defence of Poesie, 1595), Sir Philip Sidney classifies poetry into three kinds: religious (divine poetry that imitates the inconceivable excellencies of God, such as the Psalms), philosophical (didactic verse teaching moral, natural, or historical knowledge), and imaginative ('right poets' who imitate to teach and delight).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q23
items.stem:
Stephen Dedalus appears as a character in :
(A) A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
(B) Mrs. Dalloway
(C) The Voyage Out
(D) Ulysses
(E) To the Light House
items.explanation: Stephen Dedalus is James Joyce's semi-autobiographical protagonist in A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) and a central character in Ulysses (1922). The other listed novels—Mrs. Dalloway, The Voyage Out, and To the Lighthouse—were written by Virginia Woolf.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q24
items.stem: Who, among the following, wrote about Charlotte Brontë that her mind contained 'nothing but hunger, rebellion, and rage'?
items.explanation: In an April 1853 letter commenting on Charlotte Brontë's recently published novel Villette, Victorian poet and critic Matthew Arnold famously remarked that Brontë's mind contained 'nothing but hunger, rebellion, and rage.'

items.title: Mock #08 · Q25
items.stem:
The Pre-Raphaelite brotherhood -
The University Wits - The Rhymers'
Club - The Transitional Poets - The
Scottish Chaucerians.

The right chronological sequence
would be
options: The University Wits, The Scottish Chaucerians - The Pre-Raphaelite brotherhood, The Transitional Poets - The Rhymers' Club
The Rhymers' Club, The University Wits - The Scottish Chaucerians - The Transitional Poets, The Pre-Raphaelite brotherhood
The Pre-Raphaelite brotherhood - The Rhymers' Club - The Transitional Poets, The Scottish Chaucerians - The University Wits
The Scottish Chaucerians - The University Wits - The Transitional Poets - The Pre- Raphaelite brotherhood - The Rhymers' Club
items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence of these literary groups is: the Scottish Chaucerians (fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries), the University Wits (1580s–1590s), the Transitional Poets (mid-to-late eighteenth century), the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (founded in 1848), and the Rhymers' Club (founded in 1890).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q26
items.stem: Gaiutra Bahadur is a _____ writer.
items.explanation: Gaiutra Bahadur, author of Coolie Woman: The Odyssey of Indenture (2013), is a Guyanese-American journalist and writer born in Guyana who emigrated to the United States as a child.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q27
items.stem:
Which of the following assertions/assumptions are not true regarding cultures of space?
A. space is about power to control access, representation and use.
B. Space is simply land or built-up area.
C. The Space influences social relations and communities.
D. Space is socially constructed through social relations.
E. Space has nothing to do with everyday activities of people.
items.explanation: In contemporary cultural geography and spatial theory, space is understood as dynamic, socially constructed, and embedded in power relations (A, C, and D). Consequently, assuming that space is merely physical land (B) or that it is detached from everyday human practices (E) represents untrue assertions.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q28
items.stem: Name the author/writer who is not associated with British Cultural Studies.
items.explanation: I.A. Richards was a founding figure of Cambridge Practical Criticism and New Criticism, whereas Richard Hoggart, Raymond Williams, and Stuart Hall were the foundational scholars who established British Cultural Studies at the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (CCCS).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q29
items.stem:
Which among the following statements are true about Panchatantra?
A. Panchatantra is a descendant of Hitopdesha.
B. It is a manual for the instructions of the sons of a king in the principles of good conduct.
C. The first book deals with the adventures of a tortoise, deer and a cow.
D. Zantrakhyavika is one of the oldest redactions of Panchatantra.
E. Panchatantra is divided into five parts.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Vishnusharma's Panchatantra was composed as a niti-sastra manual to instruct a king's sons in statecraft and wise conduct (B), the Kashmiri Tantrakhyayika is one of its oldest surviving Sanskrit recensions (D), and it is divided into five tantras or books (E). Hitopadesha is a later descendant of the Panchatantra (making A false); thus B, D, E only.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q30
items.stem: Who among the following has authored The Revenger's Tragedie?
items.explanation: The Jacobean revenge play The Revenger's Tragedy (published anonymously in 1607) was traditionally attributed to Cyril Tourneur, though modern scholarship since the late twentieth century generally assigns it to Thomas Middleton.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q31
items.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I
(A) "Willing to wound, and yet afraid to strike."
(B) "It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man in possession of good fortune must be in want of a wife."
(C) "Thou still unravished bride of quietness, / Thou foster child of silence and slow time."
(D) "And ice, mast-high, come floating by, as green as emerald."

List II
(I) Irony
(II) Simile
(III) Antithesis
(IV) Assonance

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Alexander Pope's 'Willing to wound, and yet afraid to strike' exemplifies Antithesis (A-III); Jane Austen's opening of Pride and Prejudice exemplifies Irony (B-I); Keats's 'bride of quietness / child of silence' uses long-i Assonance (C-IV); and Coleridge's 'as green as emerald' is a Simile (D-II).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q32
items.stem: The Modern Promethean is the alternative title of
items.explanation: Mary Shelley's Gothic novel Frankenstein (1818) bears the subtitle or, The Modern Prometheus, likening Victor Frankenstein's hubristic creation of artificial life to the Greek Titan Prometheus, who fashioned humanity from clay and stole fire from heaven.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q33
items.stem:
Which of the following statements hold true with respect to Alexander Pope's "Essay on Criticism"?
A. It is "an inquiry into the nature and value of poetry".
B. It presents "a series of generalizations about good taste".
C. It explores the challenges of impartial and just criticism.
D. It underlines the traits of "the good critic".
E. It critically reflects on Plato's rejection of poetry.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A, B, C and E only
items.explanation: Alexander Pope's An Essay on Criticism (1711) presents neoclassical generalizations about good taste and 'Nature methodiz'd' (B), examines the causes of faulty and biased judgment (C), and outlines the moral and intellectual qualities of the ideal critic in Part III (D).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q34
items.stem:
Which of the following novels
depicts the plight of the Bangladeshi
immigrants in East London ?
items.explanation: Monica Ali's debut novel Brick Lane (2003), named after a street at the heart of London's Bangladeshi community, depicts the immigrant experience of Nazneen, a young Bangladeshi woman who moves to Tower Hamlets in East London after an arranged marriage.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q35
items.stem:
What is the correct sequence of the Following plays of Girish Karnad in order of their year of publication?
A. Hayavadana
B. Nagamandala
C. Tughlaq
D. Yayati
E. Bali, The Sacrifice
items.explanation: In order of composition and publication: Girish Karnad published Yayati in 1961 (D), Tughlaq in 1964 (C), Hayavadana in 1971 (A), Bali: The Sacrifice (originally written as Hittina Hunja) in 1980 (E), and Nagamandala in 1988 (B). This establishes the sequence DCAEB.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q36
items.stem: Which of these constitutes the only extant trilogy from ancient Greek tragedy?
options: King Oedipus, Oedipus at Colonus, Antigone
items.explanation: Aeschylus's 'Oresteia' (consisting of the three tragedies Agamemnon, Choephori / The Libation Bearers, and The Eumenides, performed in 458 BCE) is the only surviving complete trilogy from classical Greek drama.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q37
items.stem:
Given below are two statements :— Assertion (A) and Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : Only actual research develops research skills.
Reason (R) : Information is discrete, whereas knowledge consists of a network of connections.
In the light of the above two statements choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are independently true: hands-on practice is essential to develop research skills, and knowledge is an interconnected network rather than isolated facts. However, the distinction between information and knowledge does not directly explain why only practical research builds research skills.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q38
items.stem: Which one of the following playwrights will not be covered under the category / term 'Theatre of the Absurd' ?
items.explanation: In his landmark study The Theatre of the Absurd (1961), Martin Esslin grouped Samuel Beckett, Eugène Ionesco, and Jean Genet as major Absurdist dramatists. Jean Giraudoux (1882–1944), author of Tiger at the Gates and The Madwoman of Chaillot, belonged to an earlier French tradition of philosophical and mythic drama.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q39
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: According to Sigmund Freud, civilisation is to some extent the cumulative product of our psychology. Choose the correct option(s): (A) The purpose of human life is the pursuit of happiness. (B) Man is wholly good. (C) Abolition of private property will remove ill-will and hostility among men. (D) Creative art reflects the purpose of human life. (E) Civilisation is analogous with the human psyche. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Civilization and Its Discontents (1930), Sigmund Freud argues that human beings strive after happiness under the pleasure principle (A), creative art offers sublimated satisfaction of instinctual desires (D), and the developmental trajectory of civilization parallels that of the individual psyche (E). Statements (B) and (C) are false because Freud posited an innate aggressive drive (Thanatos) and explicitly dismissed the communist belief that abolishing private property would eliminate human aggression.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q40
items.stem:
Which English journal announced that it was "principally intended for the use of Politick
Persons who are so publick - spirited as to neglect their own Affairs to look into Transactions
of State" but failed to live up to this and amused readers with "accounts of Gallantry, Pleasure
and Entertainment " ?
items.explanation: In the opening issue of The Tatler (12 April 1709), founded by Richard Steele under the pseudonym Isaac Bickerstaff, Steele announced that the periodical was meant for 'Politick Persons' while promising to entertain the fair sex and general readers with 'Accounts of Gallantry, Pleasure, and Entertainment'.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q41
items.stem:
Match the List-I with List-II
List I (Dalit Writer):
A. Lal Singh Dil
B. Urmila Pawar
C. Tulsi Ram
D. Devanur Mahadeva

List II (Language):
I. Hindi
II. Kannada
III. Punjabi
IV. Marathi

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Dalit writers match their literary languages as follows: revolutionary poet Lal Singh Dil wrote in Punjabi (A-III), feminist author Urmila Pawar (Aaydaan / The Weave of My Life) writes in Marathi (B-IV), autobiographer Tulsi Ram (Murdahiya) wrote in Hindi (C-I), and novelist Devanoora Mahadeva (Kusumabale) writes in Kannada (D-II).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q42
items.stem: Which of the following texts has been written by Rabindranath Tagore?
items.explanation: Chandalika (1938) is a celebrated dance-drama by Rabindranath Tagore, based on the Buddhist legend of Prakriti, an untouchable young woman who falls in love with the monk Ananda, offering a profound critique of caste prejudice and spiritual rebirth.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q43
items.stem:
Which statements among the following are not relevant to Biographia Literania?

A The first volume of the text recounts the author's friendship with Robert Southey and William Blake

B. Another edition of the text was published later in 1847 with his daughter Sara's appended notes

C. Its a work by S.T. Coleridge in two volumes

D. In this work, Coleridge discusses the difference between fancy and imagination

E. In the first volume, Coleridge acknowledges his teachers and philosophers including Aristotle and Plato

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Statements A and E are not relevant: in Biographia Literaria (1817), Samuel Taylor Coleridge focuses on his literary partnership with William Wordsworth (not William Blake), and the work was annotated and edited in 1847 by his daughter Sara Coleridge (not Mary Shelley).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q44
items.stem: In Book 5 of prelude, Wordsworth dreams of an Arab in the desert after reading which great work?
items.explanation: In Book 5 ("Books") of William Wordsworth's The Prelude (1805/1850), the speaker falls asleep while reading Miguel de Cervantes's Don Quixote and dreams of an Arab phantom on a camel carrying a stone (geometry) and a shell (poetry).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q45
items.stem: Arrange the following literary journals chronologically
options: The Tatler The London Magazine The Quarterly Review Blackwood's Magazine The Saturday Review
The Tatler The Saturday Review Blackwood's Magazine The Quarterly Review The London Magazine
The Quarterly Review Blackwood's Magazine The Tatler The Saturday Review The London Magazine
The London Magazine The Quarterly Review Blackwood's Magazine The Saturday Review The Tatler
items.explanation: The correct chronological order of founding for these British periodicals is: Richard Steele's The Tatler (1709), The London Magazine (founded 1732), The Quarterly Review (1809), Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine (1817), and The Saturday Review (1855).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q46
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: “Territorialization” is a term given by-
items.explanation: Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari introduced the concept of 'territorialization' (along with deterritorialization and reterritorialization) in *Anti-Oedipus* (1972) and *A Thousand Plateaus* (1980) to describe how social regimes, habits, and spatial borders regulate and constrain desire.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q47
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Dr. Johnson had an inclination toward the Tory political ideology.
Statement II: Dr. Johnson strongly believed in transcendental scepticism.

In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Samuel Johnson was a staunch Tory and High Church Anglican in his political and religious outlook (Statement I is true), and as an empiricist and devout Christian moralist he firmly rejected transcendental scepticism (Statement II is false).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q48
items.stem:
The following lines are spoken by which character in Shakespeare's plays?
Put out the light, and then put out the light:
If I quench thee, thou flaming minister,
I can again thy former light restore
items.explanation: Othello speaks these famous lines in Act V, Scene 2 of Shakespeare's Othello (c. 1603–1604) as he enters Desdemona's bedchamber holding a candle just before extinguishing her life.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q49
items.stem:
Which of the following does the Subaltern Studies project contend?
A. Traditional historiography celebrated the role of the subalterns.
B. Traditional history of India's freedom movement celebrates the contribution of select icons.
C. Traditional historiography highlights the dominant strands of India's freedom struggle.
D. Subaltern Studies historiography highlights the dominant strands of India's freedom struggle.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Founded by Ranajit Guha in 1982, the Subaltern Studies project critiques colonial and bourgeois-nationalist historiography for celebrating only select elite icons (B) and dominant mainstream strands of India's freedom struggle (C) while erasing subaltern agency.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q50
items.stem: In many ways, grammatical categories remain mysterious. What does it mean to speak a language that in every sentence requires you to locate yourself in time, or specify your source of knowledge, or the shape of what you are talking about ? We still don't know. But putting the question like this suggests a clear and limited way of interpreting the idea that different languages represent different worlds. Which of the following statements on this passage interprets it most accurately ?
options: The passage reflects the unreliability of grammatical categories of a language generally
The passage suggests that the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis is largely discredited today
The passage upholds the reliability of grammatical categories of a language generally
The passage concedes that the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis cannot be discounted entirely
items.explanation: By noting that obligatory grammatical categories (such as tense or evidentiality) offer 'a clear and limited way of interpreting the idea that different languages represent different worlds,' the passage concedes that a qualified version of linguistic relativity (the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis) holds validity.

items.explanation: 'The squat pen rests; snug as a gun' is from Seamus Heaney's 'Digging' (I-3); 'A serious house on serious earth it is' is from Philip Larkin's 'Church Going' (II-1); 'Time held me green and dying' is from Dylan Thomas's 'Fern Hill' (III-4); and 'I hold Creation in my foot' is from Ted Hughes's 'Hawk Roosting' (IV-2).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q52
items.stem: Name the play during the performance of which the Globe Theatre was burned down in 1613.
items.explanation: On 29 June 1613, the first Globe Theatre burned to the ground when wadding from a theatrical cannon ignited the thatched roof during a performance of William Shakespeare and John Fletcher's history play Henry VIII (then titled All Is True).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q53
items.stem:
Which of the following poems are not by Robert Frost ?
(A) “An Old Man’s Winter Night”
(B) “The Grindstone”
(C) “The Smile”
(D) “Under the Balcony”
(E) “The New Remorse”
items.explanation: 'Under the Balcony' (1881) and 'The New Remorse' (1887) are poems composed by Oscar Wilde, not Robert Frost. In contrast, 'An Old Man's Winter Night' (1916), 'The Grindstone' (1923), and 'The Smile' are celebrated poems by Robert Frost.

the fragmented world of Experience
is symbolized in the image of the
items.explanation: In William Blake's poem "The Human Abstract" from Songs of Experience (1794), the Tree of Mystery grows inside the human brain, nourished by hypocrisy and fear until it bears the "dismal shade" and "fruit of Deceit."

items.title: Mock #08 · Q55
items.stem:
Arrange the following in chronological order of their year of publication:
A. Fraser’s Magazine
B. The Spectator
C. The Westminster Review
D. The Quarterly Review
E. Edinburgh Review
items.explanation: The founding dates of these British periodicals in chronological order are: The Edinburgh Review (founded 1802), the Tory periodical The Quarterly Review (founded 1809), the utilitarian Westminster Review (founded 1824), the weekly journal The Spectator (founded 1828), and Fraser's Magazine (founded 1830). This establishes the sequence E -> D -> C -> B -> A.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q56
items.stem: The medieval English university organized its studies based on the seven liberal arts. Three of these, the trivium, referred to the study of
items.explanation: The trivium was grammar, logic and rhetoric. The quadrivium was arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy.

Statement II: It is about three young men and their dog on a holiday.

In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Jerome K. Jerome's comic novel Three Men in a Boat (To Say Nothing of the Dog) (1889), originally conceived as a serialized travelogue for Home Chimes, is written in a humorous, digressive, journalistic style (Statement I is true) and recounts a Thames boating holiday taken by three friends—J., Harris, and George—along with their fox terrier Montmorency (Statement II is true).

items.explanation: Canto I of Lord Byron's satirical epic poem Don Juan (1819–24) famously opens with the lines: 'I want a hero: an uncommon want, / When every year and month sends forth a new one.'

items.explanation: The Direct Method of language teaching relies on immersion in the target language without mother-tongue translation (a), continuous oral practice and repetition (b), and accurate sentence patterns (c).

items.explanation: Virginia Woolf's extended essay A Room of One's Own (1929) laid the foundation for feminist literary criticism, famously arguing that a woman must have money and a private room of her own if she is to write fiction.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q62
items.stem: Who, amongst the following, attempted to reconcile discrepancies between various classical authors such as Plato and Aristotle, as well as between philosophy and poetry?
items.explanation: The Neoplatonists (including Plotinus, Porphyry, and Proclus) harmonized philosophical discrepancies between Plato and Aristotle, reconciling philosophy and poetry by interpreting mythological narratives and poetic symbols as allegorical expressions of higher metaphysical truth.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q63
items.stem:
Which of the following assumptions is not true with regard to Lacan’s concept/theory of standpoint?
A. It assumes that social position can provide privileged perspective on some relations and knowledge.
B. It argues that those who are marginalised or oppressed may have access to insights and perceptions that dominant group lacks.
C. It refers to a situation in which the oppressed class is destined to lose the class consciousness.
D. It suggests that the perspectives of those on the margins of society cannot help to understand social dynamics.
E. The theory is based on the idea that social contradictions and political struggle can shape counter-hegemonic norms.
items.explanation: Standpoint theory asserts that marginalized social locations provide critical epistemic advantages for understanding systemic inequality (affirming A, B, and E). Thus, the claims that the oppressed inevitably lose class consciousness (C) or that marginal perspectives fail to illuminate social dynamics (D) are untrue.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q64
items.meta: Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem:
Choose the correct statements regarding scope of linguistics from the following:
A. To describe and trace the history of all observable languages.
B. To determine the forces that are permanently and universally at work in all languages.
C. To study manifestations of civilized human speech only.
D. To consider only correct speech and flowery language.
E. To delimit and define itself.
items.explanation: Statements A, B, and E are the three fundamental tasks of linguistics explicitly defined by Ferdinand de Saussure in his *Course in General Linguistics* (1916). Statements C and D are false because modern linguistics is descriptive and universal, studying all manifestations of human speech without restricting itself to 'civilized' or 'flowery' language.

items.explanation: The correct chronological order of these prose pamphlets is: John Milton's Areopagitica (1644), Daniel Defoe's The Shortest Way with the Dissenters (1702), Jonathan Swift's A Modest Proposal (1729), and Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790).

items.title: Mock #08 · Q68

options: He discovers the way to Hell
He drowns in the River of Death
items.explanation: In John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress (1678), Ignorance is ferried across the River of Death by Vain-Hope, but because he lacks a certificate of entry at the Celestial City, two Shining Ones bind him and cast him into the door on the side of the hill leading to Hell. This prompts the concluding reflection that there is a way to Hell even from the gates of Heaven.

Production and analysis of writings by women on women
items.explanation: Coined by Elaine Showalter in 'Toward a Feminist Poetics' (1979), 'gynocriticism' defines the critical study of women as writers, focusing specifically on female literary history, themes, genres, and the production of writings by women on women.

items.explanation: In classical rhetoric, 'enumeration' (enumeratio) is the device of listing or detailing multiple parts, causes, or attributes of a subject one after another—here, cataloguing the beloved's eyes, hair, nose, cheeks, and lips for rhetorical emphasis.

items.explanation: John Keats's narrative poem Isabella; or, The Pot of Basil (1818, published 1820) adapts a tale from Giovanni Boccaccio's Decameron (Day IV, Story 5) and was originally intended for a collaborative volume of versified Boccaccio stories with John Hamilton Reynolds.

items.explanation: Claude Lévi-Strauss introduced the concept of 'bricolage' (and the figure of the 'bricoleur') in *The Savage Mind* (*La Pensée sauvage*, 1962) to describe how mythical and cultural systems are assembled using whatever symbolic fragments and resources are at hand.

items.explanation: Mikhail Bakhtin theorized dialogism as an intrinsic property of living language (A-III); Michel Foucault authored The Order of Things: An Archaeology of the Human Sciences (1966) (B-I); Roland Barthes distinguished between readerly (lisible) and writerly (scriptible) texts in S/Z (1970) (C-II); and Sigmund Freud explored dreams and the unconscious in The Interpretation of Dreams (1899) (D-IV). items.title: Mock #08 · Q91
items.stem:
Read the following poem and answer the questions that follow:

Apostrophe to Man
(on reflecting that the world is ready to go to war again)

Detestable race, continue to expunge yourself, die out.
Breed faster, crowd, encroach, sing hymns, build bombing airplanes;
Make speeches, unveil statues, make more bombs, hide more bombs
In the mountains, in the caves of the mountains,
The high, deep-buried caves,
Under the rock and ice.
Breed, crowd, encroach, expand, expunge yourself, die out,
Homo called sapiens.
Put death on the market:
Convert again into explosives the bewildered ammonia and the distracted cellulose;
Convert again into putrescent matter drawing flies
The hopeful bodies of the young; exhort,
Pray, pull long faces, be earnest, be all but overcome, be photographed;
Confer, perfect your formulae, commercialize
Bacteria harmful to human tissue.
Put death on the market;
Breed, crowd, encroach, expand, expunge yourself, die out,
Homo called sapiens.

What is the meaning of the word ‘detestable’ in the context of the poem?
items.explanation: In the opening line of Edna St. Vincent Millay's 'Apostrophe to Man' ('Detestable race, continue to expunge yourself, die out'), the word 'detestable' means deserving intense hatred, scorn, and contempt, making it synonymous with 'contemptible'.

Confer, perfect your formulae, commercialize
Bacteria harmful to human tissue.
Put death on the market;
Breed, crowd, encroach, expand, expunge yourself, die out,
Homo called sapiens.

The last line — ‘Breed, crowd, encroach, expand, expunge yourself, die out’ has the figurative device termed:
items.explanation: The line 'Breed, crowd, encroach, expand, expunge yourself, die out' employs alliteration (printed in the examination paper options as 'Alteration'), repeating the initial vowel and consonant sounds in 'encroach, expand, expunge'.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q95
items.stem:
Read the following poem and answer the questions that follow:

Apostrophe to Man
(on reflecting that the world is ready to go to war again)

Detestable race, continue to expunge yourself, die out.
Breed faster, crowd, encroach, sing hymns, build bombing airplanes;
Make speeches, unveil statues, make more bombs, hide more bombs
In the mountains, in the caves of the mountains,
The high, deep-buried caves,
Under the rock and ice.
Breed, crowd, encroach, expand, expunge yourself, die out,
Homo called sapiens.
Put death on the market:
Convert again into explosives the bewildered ammonia and the distracted cellulose;
Convert again into putrescent matter drawing flies
The hopeful bodies of the young; exhort,
Pray, pull long faces, be earnest, be all but overcome, be photographed;
Confer, perfect your formulae, commercialize
Bacteria harmful to human tissue.
Put death on the market;
Breed, crowd, encroach, expand, expunge yourself, die out,
Homo called sapiens.

The title of the poem ‘Apostrophe to Man’ is ______ in the context of the overall content.
options: a eulogy and ode to homo sapiens
items.explanation: The formal classical title 'Apostrophe to Man' functions ironically and satirically, addressing mankind as 'Homo called sapiens' while savagely exposing humanity's irrational, self-destructive race toward annihilation.

items.title: Mock #08 · Q96
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:

Emergent in the wake of industrialization, studies of everyday life endeavor to bring into visibility and somehow make sense of our humble, taken-for-granted, seemingly unremarkable experience of the quotidian. The project has meant subjecting modern Western individuals to the kind of anthropological scrutiny more often reserved for non-Western peoples. The goal has been to explore patterns of behavior not because they are foreign but because they are so familiar as to fall beneath our notice. Artists as well as social theorists in this tradition set out to register and evaluate the neglected minutiae of our daily lives: the ways we sleep and ambulate, ingest and eliminate, work and recreate, care for ourselves and others, slip in and out of self-awareness, and interact with people, objects, and our surroundings.

Generally speaking, everyday life studies is a science of the "small." Though usually framed in relation to larger social structures, the objects of attention are micro-moments and micro-actions — turning a street corner, stirring a pot, feeding an infant. They are actions that take place without rising to the status of "event." They are moments in time that leave no historical mark (at least as "history" has traditionally been understood). As these examples suggest, such practices are "everyday" not only because they are "ordinary" but also because they typically occur every day, perhaps even every few hours. Whether tied to bodily rhythms or the rigors of wage work, the non-events of everyday life are almost always characterized by patterns of repetition.

Theorists of the everyday, focusing on the effects of modernity, have taken various stances on the political implications of our daily routines. Some have tied their repetitive nature to the mechanization and alienation of labor in a capitalist society. For Michel Foucault, domination is not restricted to the factory floor: the workings of power are more diffuse and insidious than this, operating in the very interstices of our seemingly private lives. For Michel de Certeau, the quotidian is a site not of forcible conformity but of micro-opportunities to defy the dominant order.

‘Everyday life’ as a theory deals with:
options: Events that are part of history's grand narratives
Events that are mundane and steeped in banality
Events that are epochal to the life of a community or nation
items.explanation: As stated in the passage, everyday life studies investigates our humble, taken-for-granted experience and focuses on micro-actions that occur without rising to the status of a grand historical event, dealing with moments that are mundane and steeped in banality.

items.explanation: The term 'quotidian' derives from the Latin for 'every day' and refers to the recurring, unremarkable practices, routines, and experiences of daily life.

options: Because it deals only and exclusively with the lives of disenfranchised subjects.
Because it is anthropological in methodology, and therefore a ‘small’ science.

items.explanation: The passage explains that everyday life studies is a 'science of the small' because its objects of attention are ordinary micro-moments and repetitive micro-actions—such as turning a corner, stirring a pot, or feeding an infant—that form part of mundane daily processes.

What is not related to the meaning of ‘interstice’?
items.explanation: An 'interstice' is an intervening space, gap, fissure, or crevice—spaces associated with in-betweenness, ambivalence, and slippage; 'monolithic' (meaning massive, solid, uniform, and unbroken) is an antonym and unrelated in meaning.
